note: Complaint-oriented entries. Each maps a presenting complaint to traditional self-care, the diet and lifestyle advice that goes with it, and the point at which self-care stops and a doctor is needed. Keywords include Hindi/Hinglish terms because patients describe symptoms in their own language.

documents.title: Common cold, cough and sore throat
documents.text: An uncomplicated cold and cough is usually viral and settles in 5-7 days with rest, warm fluids and steam. Traditional care centres on tulsi-ginger kadha, steam inhalation, salt-water gargling for throat pain, and turmeric milk at night. Honey with ginger juice is the standard household cough syrup for adults and children over one year.
documents.self_care: Tulsi-ginger-black pepper kadha twice daily. Steam inhalation 2-3 times a day. Warm salt-water gargle for sore throat, 3-4 times daily. 1 tsp honey with a few drops of ginger juice for cough. Turmeric milk at night. Plenty of warm fluids and rest.
documents.diet: Warm, light, freshly cooked food. Avoid cold drinks, curd at night, fried and heavy food. Ginger tea, soups and khichdi suit this phase.
documents.escalate: See a doctor if fever crosses 5 days, if there is breathlessness or chest pain, if cough produces blood, if the person is elderly or has asthma/COPD/diabetes, or if a child is feeding poorly or unusually drowsy.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Fever (uncomplicated)
documents.text: Most short-lived fevers are viral and self-limiting. Traditional care focuses on hydration, rest and light food, with giloy used for recurrent or lingering low-grade fever. The important clinical judgement is not the remedy but recognising the fevers that are not simple: those with rash, severe headache, neck stiffness, confusion, breathlessness or that persist beyond a few days.
documents.self_care: Rest and generous fluids — water, coconut water, thin dal water, ORS. Tepid sponging if the temperature is high and uncomfortable. Giloy decoction for lingering or recurring low-grade fever. Light, easily digested food.
documents.diet: Khichdi, moong dal soup, rice water, fruit. Avoid heavy, oily and fried food while the fever lasts.
documents.escalate: Urgent review for fever with confusion or drowsiness, severe headache with neck stiffness, breathlessness, rash that does not blanch, bleeding gums or nose, very low urine output, fever over 5 days, or fever in pregnancy, infancy or immunocompromise. In dengue-prone seasons, falling platelets need medical monitoring.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Acidity, heartburn and reflux
documents.text: Acidity presents as burning behind the breastbone or in the upper abdomen, sour belching and discomfort that is worse when lying down or after spicy or late meals. Traditional care uses cooling, demulcent remedies together with meal-timing correction, which is usually the more important half of the treatment.
documents.self_care: Cold milk or coconut water for immediate relief. Amla juice or powder in the morning. Soaked fennel (saunf) or a fennel decoction after meals. Mulethi is soothing but must be avoided if the person has high blood pressure. Sleep with the head end of the bed raised.
documents.diet: Eat dinner by 7-8 pm and at least 3 hours before lying down. Smaller, more frequent meals. Cut chillies, deep-fried food, excess tea/coffee, alcohol and smoking. Include banana, cucumber, coconut water and buttermilk.
documents.escalate: Important: burning chest pain can be cardiac, not gastric. Seek emergency care if chest discomfort comes with sweating, breathlessness, or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back — especially over age 40 or with diabetes or hypertension. Also see a doctor for difficulty swallowing, vomiting blood, black stools, unexplained weight loss, or symptoms not settling in 2 weeks.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Indigestion, gas and bloating
documents.text: Bloating and heaviness after meals usually reflect weak digestion (mandagni in Ayurvedic terms), eating too fast, or an irregular meal schedule. Carminative spices already present in most Indian kitchens are the traditional answer, alongside correcting how and when the person eats.
documents.self_care: Ajwain with a pinch of black salt in warm water after meals. Roasted jeera powder in buttermilk. A small piece of fresh ginger with rock salt before meals to kindle digestion. A 10-15 minute gentle walk after dinner. Vajrasana for 5 minutes after meals.
documents.diet: Eat at fixed times, chew properly, avoid drinking large amounts of water during meals. Reduce raw salads at night, cold food, carbonated drinks, maida and heavy dairy. Warm cooked food suits better.
documents.escalate: See a doctor for persistent abdominal pain, vomiting, blood in stool, black stools, unexplained weight loss, a change in bowel habit lasting weeks, or bloating with severe pain and inability to pass stool or gas.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Constipation
documents.text: Chronic constipation in the absence of alarm features responds mostly to fibre, fluid and routine rather than to laxatives. Triphala is the classical remedy and is regarded as safe for longer-term use, unlike stimulant laxatives which the gut becomes dependent on.
documents.self_care: Triphala 1 tsp in warm water at bedtime. Warm water on waking. Soaked raisins or figs, or 1-2 tsp of ghee in warm milk at night. Regular toilet timing, ideally the same time each morning without hurry.
documents.diet: More fibre — whole grains, vegetables, fruit with skin, soaked seeds. 2.5-3 litres of water a day unless fluid-restricted. Reduce maida, biscuits and processed food. Regular physical activity matters as much as diet.
documents.escalate: See a doctor for constipation with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, blood in stool, a new change in bowel habit after age 45, unexplained weight loss, or complete inability to pass stool and gas — which can indicate obstruction and is urgent.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Headache and migraine
documents.text: Most headaches are tension-type or migraine. Tension headache is a band-like pressure linked to stress, poor sleep, screen strain or skipped meals; migraine is typically one-sided and throbbing with nausea and light sensitivity. Traditional care targets triggers and provides cooling, calming measures.
documents.self_care: For tension headache: warm oil head massage (brahmi or coconut oil), neck and shoulder stretches, screen breaks, adequate sleep. For migraine: rest in a dark quiet room, cold compress on the forehead, ginger tea for the nausea. Anulom-vilom pranayama 10 minutes daily as prevention. Brahmi is used as a longer-term calming herb.
documents.diet: Do not skip meals — a skipped meal is a common migraine trigger. Identify and avoid personal triggers such as fermented food, aged cheese, MSG, excess caffeine or chocolate. Keep hydration steady.
documents.escalate: Emergency assessment for a sudden severe 'worst ever' headache, headache with fever and neck stiffness, headache with weakness, numbness, slurred speech or vision loss, headache after a head injury, or a new persistent headache after age 50. These can indicate bleeding, infection or stroke.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Insomnia and poor sleep
documents.text: Difficulty falling or staying asleep is usually driven by stress, irregular sleep timing, late screens, caffeine or late heavy meals. Traditional care combines a calming night routine with nervine herbs, and works best when sleep timing is regularised first.
documents.self_care: Ashwagandha 3-5 g in warm milk at night. Warm oil massage to the soles of the feet and scalp before bed. Fixed sleep and wake times, including weekends. No screens for an hour before bed. Bhramari pranayama 5-10 rounds at bedtime. Nutmeg (a pinch) in warm milk is a traditional addition.
documents.diet: Light early dinner, ideally by 7-8 pm. No caffeine after 4 pm. Avoid alcohol as a sleep aid — it fragments sleep later in the night.
documents.escalate: See a doctor if insomnia persists beyond a few weeks despite good sleep habits, if there is loud snoring with daytime sleepiness or witnessed breathing pauses (possible sleep apnoea), or if poor sleep comes with low mood, loss of interest or thoughts of self-harm — which needs prompt professional support.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Stress and anxiety
documents.text: Persistent stress and anxiety often present physically — palpitations, tight chest, disturbed sleep, appetite change, headaches or gut upset. Traditional care uses adaptogenic and nervine herbs together with breathing practice, and it is important to distinguish anxiety symptoms from cardiac or thyroid causes when the presentation is physical.
documents.self_care: Ashwagandha 3-5 g at night. Brahmi for the mental restlessness component. Anulom-vilom and bhramari pranayama 10-15 minutes daily. Regular physical activity. A consistent daily routine (dinacharya) is considered central, not optional.
documents.diet: Regular meals, reduced caffeine, adequate magnesium-rich food such as nuts, seeds and green leafy vegetables. Avoid alcohol and tobacco as coping strategies.
documents.escalate: Seek professional help for panic attacks, anxiety that stops normal functioning, low mood lasting more than two weeks, or any thoughts of self-harm — in India the Tele-MANAS helpline is 14416 and the mental-health helpline 9152987821. New palpitations or chest tightness should be medically assessed to rule out cardiac or thyroid causes before being attributed to anxiety.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Joint pain and arthritis
documents.text: Joint pain with morning stiffness that eases with movement suggests an inflammatory pattern; pain that worsens through the day with use suggests a wear-related pattern. Traditional care combines internal anti-inflammatories with external oil application and joint-appropriate movement — rest alone tends to worsen stiffness.
documents.self_care: Turmeric milk with black pepper and ghee at night. Warm sesame oil or mahanarayan oil massage to the joint, followed by warm fomentation. Gentle daily range-of-motion exercise. Weight reduction where the knees are affected makes the largest practical difference.
documents.diet: Anti-inflammatory pattern — whole grains, vegetables, turmeric, ginger, omega-3 sources. Reduce refined sugar, fried food and excess red meat. For gout specifically, reduce organ meat, shellfish and alcohol.
documents.escalate: See a doctor for a hot, red, acutely swollen joint (possible infection — this is urgent), joint pain with fever, morning stiffness lasting over an hour, joint pain with rash or weight loss, or pain that is not improving over 3-4 weeks of self-care.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Low back pain
documents.text: Most low back pain is mechanical and improves within a few weeks. The key traditional and modern advice agree: stay gently active rather than resting in bed, apply local warmth and oil, and correct posture and lifting technique.
documents.self_care: Warm sesame or mahanarayan oil massage followed by hot fomentation. Gentle stretching and core-strengthening; bhujangasana and marjariasana as tolerated. Avoid prolonged sitting — stand and move every 30-40 minutes. A firm mattress and correct lifting posture.
documents.diet: Adequate calcium and vitamin D. Maintain a healthy weight to reduce lumbar load.
documents.escalate: Urgent assessment for back pain with numbness in the inner thighs or groin, loss of bladder or bowel control, progressive leg weakness, back pain after a fall or injury, back pain with fever, or unexplained weight loss with night pain. These suggest nerve compression, infection or other serious causes.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: High blood pressure — lifestyle support
documents.text: Hypertension is usually symptomless, which is why measurement matters more than how a person feels. Traditional support — Arjuna, stress reduction, salt reduction — is genuinely useful, but it is adjunctive: prescribed antihypertensive medication should never be stopped or replaced on the basis of herbal treatment.
documents.self_care: Arjuna bark powder 1-3 g with warm milk once daily as supportive care. Regular pranayama and meditation. 30-40 minutes of brisk walking most days. Adequate sleep. Home BP monitoring with a record the doctor can review.
documents.diet: Salt under 5 g/day — the main practical step is cutting pickles, papad, packaged snacks and restaurant food rather than the salt shaker alone. More potassium-rich food (banana, coconut water, leafy vegetables) unless the kidneys are impaired. Reduce alcohol; stop tobacco.
documents.escalate: Critical: licorice (mulethi) must be avoided in hypertension, as it raises blood pressure directly. Seek urgent care for BP with severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, visual disturbance, weakness on one side or confusion — these suggest a hypertensive emergency.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Type 2 diabetes — diet and lifestyle support
documents.text: Diet, activity and weight are the foundation of type 2 diabetes control, with traditional additions such as fenugreek and neem playing a supporting role. The essential safety point is that these lower blood sugar in their own right, so combining them with prescribed medication requires glucose monitoring to avoid hypoglycaemia.
documents.self_care: Soaked fenugreek seeds with the water on an empty stomach each morning. Regular post-meal walking, which blunts the sugar spike more effectively than the same walk at another time. Weight reduction where relevant. Regular glucose monitoring, foot checks and annual eye review.
documents.diet: Whole grains instead of refined; millets, oats, whole wheat. Half the plate as non-starchy vegetables. Protein at each meal. Cut sugar, sweets, fruit juice, white rice in large portions and packaged snacks. Fixed meal timings matter as much as content.
documents.escalate: Seek urgent care for symptoms of very high sugar — excessive thirst, frequent urination, rapid weight loss, drowsiness, fruity breath, abdominal pain — or of hypoglycaemia: sweating, trembling, confusion, palpitations, which need immediate sugar intake. Any non-healing foot ulcer needs prompt medical attention.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: High cholesterol
documents.text: Raised cholesterol is symptomless and managed through diet, activity, weight and — where risk is high — prescribed medication. Traditional support includes Arjuna, fenugreek, garlic and amla, used alongside rather than instead of prescribed therapy.
documents.self_care: Arjuna as cardiac support. Fenugreek seeds soaked overnight. Garlic in daily cooking. 30-45 minutes of aerobic activity most days. Stop tobacco — it lowers protective HDL.
documents.diet: Replace fried and vanaspati-based food with steamed, grilled or lightly sautéed preparations. More soluble fibre — oats, barley, legumes, apples. Nuts and seeds in moderation. Reduce refined carbohydrate, which drives triglycerides more than dietary fat does.
documents.escalate: Anyone with known heart disease, diabetes, or a strong family history of early cardiac events should be assessed by a physician for whether medication is indicated — this is not a decision to make on lifestyle grounds alone.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Anaemia and persistent fatigue
documents.text: Persistent tiredness with pallor, breathlessness on exertion, palpitations or hair fall commonly reflects iron-deficiency anaemia, which is very prevalent in India, particularly among women of reproductive age. Traditional iron-supporting foods help, but the cause of the deficiency still needs identifying rather than only treating the number.
documents.self_care: Amla for vitamin C, which substantially improves iron absorption. Dates, raisins, jaggery, sesame seeds. Cooking in an iron vessel. Take iron-rich food with a vitamin C source and away from tea or coffee, which block absorption.
documents.diet: Green leafy vegetables, legumes, jaggery, dates, sesame; pair with lemon or amla. Avoid tea/coffee within an hour of meals. Include protein adequately.
documents.escalate: Anaemia needs a cause, not just a supplement. See a doctor for blood tests if fatigue is persistent — especially with heavy menstrual bleeding, black stools, blood in stool, weight loss, or in men and post-menopausal women, where gastrointestinal blood loss must be excluded. Severe breathlessness, chest pain or fainting needs urgent care.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Acne and common skin problems
documents.text: Acne, itching and fungal skin problems are among the most common complaints seen in general practice. Traditional care uses neem and turmeric internally and externally, along with attention to hygiene, diet and — in the case of persistent fungal infection — keeping the area dry, which matters more than any remedy.
documents.self_care: Neem leaf paste or neem-boiled water wash for acne and itching. Turmeric with a little water or honey as a spot application. Aloe vera gel for irritation and dryness. Wash and fully dry skin folds; wear loose cotton clothing in humid weather.
documents.diet: Reduce refined sugar and high-glycaemic food, which worsen acne. Adequate water. Some people find dairy aggravates acne. More vegetables, fruit and omega-3 sources.
documents.escalate: See a doctor for spreading redness with fever (possible cellulitis — urgent), a rapidly spreading rash, blistering, a rash that does not blanch under pressure, painful cystic acne that scars, or any skin lesion that is changing in size, shape or colour. Recurrent fungal infection can be the first sign of undiagnosed diabetes and warrants a sugar test.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Menstrual irregularity and PCOS
documents.text: Irregular cycles, painful periods and PCOS are common presentations. In PCOS specifically, weight, insulin resistance and activity are the levers with the strongest effect, and traditional herbs such as Shatavari are supportive alongside them. Painful periods respond well to local warmth and anti-inflammatory measures.
documents.self_care: Shatavari as a general reproductive tonic. For cramps: hot water bottle on the lower abdomen, ginger tea, gentle yoga such as supta baddha konasana and bhujangasana. For PCOS: regular exercise, weight reduction where relevant, fenugreek and cinnamon for insulin sensitivity.
documents.diet: For PCOS, a lower-glycaemic pattern — whole grains, protein at each meal, reduced sugar and refined carbohydrate. Adequate iron and protein where bleeding is heavy.
documents.escalate: See a doctor for very heavy bleeding (soaking a pad hourly, or clots), bleeding between periods or after intercourse, periods absent for three or more months outside pregnancy, severe pain not relieved by usual measures, or any bleeding after menopause — the last always needs evaluation.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Loose motions and diarrhoea
documents.text: Acute diarrhoea is usually infective or dietary and settles in a few days. The priority is rehydration, not stopping the stool — anti-motility measures can be harmful in infective diarrhoea. Traditional care uses buttermilk, rice water and pomegranate.
documents.self_care: ORS after each loose stool — this is the single most important measure. Rice water (mand), buttermilk with roasted jeera, pomegranate juice. Continue eating small light meals; do not fast. Careful hand hygiene to protect the household.
documents.diet: Khichdi, curd rice, banana, boiled potato, toast. Avoid milk (other than curd/buttermilk), fried, spicy and high-fibre food until settled.
documents.escalate: Urgent care for blood or mucus in stool, high fever, severe abdominal pain, signs of dehydration (very low urine output, sunken eyes, dizziness on standing, dry mouth), diarrhoea over 3 days, or any diarrhoea in an infant, elderly or immunocompromised person. Triphala must be stopped during acute diarrhoea.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Weight management
documents.text: Sustainable weight reduction comes from a modest consistent calorie deficit, adequate protein, and activity that a person can maintain — not from short crash regimens. Traditional support includes warm water with honey and lemon, Triphala and specific yoga practice, but these are adjuncts to the underlying diet and activity change.
documents.self_care: Warm water with lemon on waking. Triphala at night if digestion is sluggish. 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly plus two sessions of strength work. Surya namaskar as a daily base practice. Adequate sleep — short sleep reliably worsens appetite regulation.
documents.diet: Fixed meal timings, protein at every meal, half the plate vegetables, whole grains over refined. Cut sugary drinks, packaged snacks and late-night eating. Portion control matters more than eliminating any single food group.
documents.escalate: See a doctor for rapid unexplained weight gain or loss, weight gain with fatigue, cold intolerance and hair fall (possible hypothyroidism), or where BMI is in the obese range with existing diabetes, hypertension or joint disease — those benefit from a supervised plan.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Breathlessness, wheezing and asthma
documents.text: Wheeze and breathlessness that recur, worsen at night or with cold air, dust or exertion suggest asthma. Traditional support includes tulsi, turmeric and steam, and pranayama has a genuine role in breathing control — but prescribed inhalers must never be replaced by herbal treatment, and any new or worsening breathlessness needs medical assessment first.
documents.self_care: Steam inhalation. Tulsi kadha. Turmeric milk. Anulom-vilom and controlled breathing practice daily, when well rather than during an attack. Identify and reduce triggers — dust, smoke, cold air, strong smells.
documents.diet: Warm, light food. Avoid cold and refrigerated items, and any personally identified food triggers. Maintain hydration to keep secretions loose.
documents.escalate: Emergency: severe breathlessness, inability to complete a sentence, blue lips, chest pain with breathlessness, or a reliever inhaler not working — call 108. Any first episode of breathlessness, or breathlessness with leg swelling or chest pain, needs prompt medical evaluation for cardiac causes.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice

documents.title: Burning urination and urinary complaints
documents.text: Burning on passing urine with frequency and urgency commonly indicates a urinary tract infection, more often in women. Traditional care emphasises flushing with fluids and cooling drinks, but a UTI with fever or back pain has usually reached the kidney and needs prompt medical treatment rather than home care.
documents.self_care: Generous water intake. Coconut water, barley water, and unsweetened cranberry where available. Punarnava as a traditional urinary support herb. Do not hold urine; pass urine after intercourse.
documents.diet: Plenty of fluids. Reduce caffeine, alcohol and spicy food while symptomatic.
documents.escalate: See a doctor promptly for fever with urinary symptoms, pain in the flank or back, blood in urine, vomiting, symptoms in a man, in pregnancy, in a child, or in diabetes — these need proper assessment and usually antibiotics. Inability to pass urine at all is an emergency.
documents.source: AYUSH home-remedy guidance; standard primary-care practice
